mechanism: Rising real yield raises gold's opportunity cost; real-money allocators (pensions, insurers) rotate out of zero-coupon gold into competitively-yielding TIPS, selling gold.
Rising inflation breakevens push macro funds to buy gold as an inflation hedge; the seller is a fixed-income holder unwilling to bear the eroding real value of coupons unhedged.

This spread widens when real yields rise and breakevens fall together, doubling the carrying-cost signal; extreme readings catch regime shifts the single real-yield series misses, same seller as DFII10.
Elevated 3-month vol pricing signals sustained macro stress; slower-moving allocators (pensions, sovereign funds) rotate into gold as a multi-month hedge, distinct from the fast spot-VIX reaction.

Gold is dollar-quoted; a rising broad trade-weighted dollar mechanically raises gold's local-currency price for non-US buyers (Indian/Chinese jewelry demand, EM central banks), and those price-sensitive buyers step back, leaving USD-based sellers in control.

Same dollar repricing hits silver, but silver's buyer base is EM industrial users who are price-takers in USD and more elastic than gold jewelry buyers, so a strengthening dollar chokes off marginal industrial demand faster.
Term-structure inversion (near-term vol jumping above far-term) marks acute equity stress; the loser is the yen-funded carry trader forced to unwind fast, buying back yen and pulling USDJPY down.

When real yield sits well above breakeven inflation, TIPS offer a compensated real return gold can't match since gold pays no coupon; the loser is the real-money allocator who rotates out of gold into TIPS while that spread stays rich.

A sustained rise in long-run inflation breakevens signals debasement expectations; the loser is the cash/bond holder watching real purchasing power erode who rotates into gold as the zero-coupon inflation hedge, a slow real-money flow that needs the longer hold to show up.
When real yield sits far above breakeven, TIPS carry beats gold's zero coupon; pension and insurance allocators slowly shift the marginal dollar from gold into TIPS over weeks.

Silver's buyers are mostly non-US industrial/retail; a high dollar percentile makes it locally expensive abroad, foreign demand steps back, and the marginal seller is a domestic long facing thin demand.
